utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, this is IT-95-14/2-T. The Prosector versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Paragraph, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's going to be paragraph 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But first I will ask the witness, Colonel Morsink, whose diaries were made available to the defence overnight, which were returned to him, as promised, at half past eight this morning. I asked him if he's been able to research those diaries for any precise records of what was said by Cerkez on the 24th of May, the subject of paragraph 68.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found those paragraphs, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This relates to what was said by Cerkez at the Vitez local commission. Can you tell us now, please, what Mr. Cerkez did say?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that the discussion was quite intense. Allegations that the ABiH was bringing in new troops, reinforcements from Opara through a small mountain trail, and this claim from Mr. Cerkez. And he said that as a reaction to that the HVO is willing to burn all Krusica down. And he explained to me that two women and one child were killed at the front line. He said that if they won't warn them, we will have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Burning Kruscica based on what? Was this a military explanation he gave you or something else?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the allegations that the ABiH were bringing in new troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Kruscica a military target, in the sense that it was a fortification or a base for --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kruscica was a stronghold held by forces of the ABiH, part of the 325 Mountain Brigade, under the command of Mr. Sifet Sivro. And I guess that there is some threat, if there really are fresh troops coming in, but nevertheless, I think you can never threaten to burn a whole village down only because of a military threat. It's part of the Geneva Convention not to threaten or bring civilian houses or civilian people in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are looking at your note on the ELMO, underneath the passage where it says the HVO is willing to burn all Kruscica down. Then there is a reference to two women and one child killed. The next line reads how, please?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They claim that one man, a HVO man, is imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The line above that. The highlighted line.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we won't warn, then we will have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn on now, then, back to where we were yesterday. Paragraph 78 in the summary. I would be grateful if you wouldn't turn to the summary. It may be difficult, but try and turn your mind to a particular date. And the particular date I want you to deal with is the 31st of May, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I am sorry to interrupt you, but we have these witness's notes, this threat issued by Mr. Cerkez. Could we -- could the witness tell us about the context within which those threats were worded? Was Mr. Cerkez expecting something, because we are given this information, but we know nothing beyond the information. We do not have the context in which this was done. So the Chamber would like to know within what context this conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the context was given yesterday, and this was completing it. But please remind us, Colonel, the context of these threats was what?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a discussion for a long time about the encirclement of Kruscica. Kruscica is a small village at the outskirts of Vitez. It's the hillside. If you look at from a perspective of Vitez itself, from the vicinity of Vitez, then you could say that Kruscica is encircled. If you see it from a larger perspective, then one could say that the whole vicinity of Vitez is encircled because of all the mountains around Vitez being controlled by ABiH. This discussion took a lot of time, every day, every meeting, and our point of view was to break the human blockade in Kruscica so that we could be able to bring the humanitarian aid into Kruscica. And the HVO side found new excuses, almost every meeting, not to be able to break this blockade. One of the new excuses was that there was new troops coming in from Opara, that means through the hills into Kruscica. So the HVO explained to us that they experienced a danger coming from Kruscica if this wasn't stopped by us. So they asked us to stop new troops coming into Kruscica. And the threats after that was that if we could not stop it and this policy of reinforcements went on, then HVO was willing to burn Kruscica down. The fact is, that there were more than 5.000 people in Kruscica, civilians, approximately one and a half thousand original inhabitants, and approximately 3.000 refugees coming from outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the witness think that the HVO had the -- Mr. Cerkez and the HVO had the means necessary to make this threat true?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a lot of artillery available and they had quite a large number of troops in Vitez. And they already showed in other villages that they were able to burn them down. So I think they were capable of doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at that moment they were held in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ABiH was held in Kruscica itself, but the front line was more or less half around Kruscica and the back side was covered by the hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the military situation is that the HVO was encircled in Kruscica, which was in the hands of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The threat about war, Colonel. Did Mr. Cerkez, as it appears on the transcript, say, "If we want war we will have it," or was it, "If they want war, they will have it"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote down during that meeting in my notes, "If we want war, then we will have it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel, if we move forward now to the 31st of May, when there was a meeting of the local commission in Kacuni of the Busovaca local commission, was there, at that meeting, an imam present?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Enver -- I forgot his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, if he contributed anything particular to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that he complained about his lack of freedom of movement. Freedom of movement was promised to him during one of the previous meetings and he still hadn't got it, and he claimed that this order came from Mr. Kordic. His car was taken away. He was not allowed to walk freely on the roads in Busovaca. There was a curfew especially for him and for his -- for the Muslims in Busovaca, and this curfew was not active for the local Croats in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, haven't we heard evidence about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be, but it's not a matter that's agreed, and therefore I've been asked specifically to deal with it in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it can be taken fairly briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I've dealt with that, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On a similar basis, just "Yes" or "No", was this meeting the subject of Croatian television and radio broadcasts in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the broadcasts accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told later on by the ABiH side and by Muslim representatives and by my interpreter --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I must object to this. I don't mean to interrupt the Colonel, but this sounds like double hearsay, because I think the Colonel is saying that he was told about these broadcasts by someone else. So you have the person telling the Colonel about what was supposedly said on the television broadcasts or radio broadcasts. Once again, consistent with our prior position, we have no objection to the introduction of any tapes or videotapes of those programmes or broadcasts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You couldn't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We agree. This is evidence very much at second-hand, and in this particular case, we don't think it assists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact, I think the witness was protesting that the characterisation is double hearsay, and I would have preferred the witness to have explained his source of information before the ruling. But if the Chamber would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You may have done; we didn't ask for it. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move to the 1st of June, which is, I think, a Muslim holiday on that year. Mr. Alagic, the commander of -- and I'm going to -- sorry, can I interrupt? The next series of paragraphs, I'm told, are not the subject of contention. In order to make speed, I'm going to read rather more even than yesterday. Colonel Morsink, if you would attend to what I'm reading from the summary and confine yourself to answering "Yes", if it's accurate, and correcting things that are substantially or significantly in error, we'll make a bit of quick speed. On the night of the 1st of June, Bajram, a Muslim holiday, Mr. Alagic, the commander of the operational group, ABiH Travnik, called a meeting because he had been stopped at an HVO checkpoint. He had been disarmed, as had his bodyguards. His vehicle and property had been stolen. The HVO soldier who took possession of the car, a person called Zute, had been sought out later and had agreed to return the property to Alagic on the orders of Nakic. Later, Blaskic, through Alistair Duncan, sent his apologies to Alagic for what had happened at this irregular checkpoint and these uncontrolled elements, this being an execution repeatedly used by the HVO whenever crimes and atrocities were committed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 82. Large-scale atrocities, in which Muslim villages or selected Muslim parts of villages in Central Bosnia had been burned, could not, in your judgement, be attributed to uncontrolled elements because the HVO in Central Bosnia, under Blaskic's command, had enough soldiers and police to eliminate uncontrolled elements, again in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning to the 2nd of June, was there a meeting of the joint command headquarters at Travnik, the situation in the city being very tense, the ABiH having taken over a lot of the city buildings, and the HVO complaining about the taking of various things? Were the allegations of the HVO investigated, turning out to be unfounded yet again?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The main item was the Dom HVO. That's the main building of the HVO, and this building was claimed to be destroyed. We visited the building. A few items were stolen, but the building was intact and was usable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had anti-tank rockets hit the Solitar and Gorazde apartment buildings, and did you establish that the rounds had been fired from the HVO barracks at Bilici, and did a joint ABiH and HVO police force guard those buildings at night, with Merdan suggesting a joint patrol for the whole city?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this same day, the 2nd of June, did both sides complain that Blaskic and Hadzihasanovic never attended the Travnik joint command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At a follow-up meeting on the 3rd of June in Travnik, was it revealed that the joint patrol of the previous night had been effective, the HVO claiming that more Croats had been forced from their houses, however, fighting breaking out from the HVO side at Han Bila?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Alagic stated he had restrained his troops and stopped them fighting back?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well. He was concerned about the front lines towards the Bosnian Serb army, where still HVO and ABiH forces were fighting together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Travnik, were there a number of complaints made in relation to stamps and flags used by the HVO, the ABiH feeling that the flags and stamps of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as internationally recognised, should be used and not the ones using the Croat chequerboard?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you return to Vitez, to be informed that Blaskic had appointed five liaison officers for Travnik, Busovaca, Vitez, and one at his own level?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That only, I think, makes four. In any case, liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then there's one place missing. As I recall it, it's Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, and one for his own operational zone level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 4th of June, did the situation in Travnik deteriorate, with roadblocks and a number of mines on the road and the starting of shooting and shelling?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There was intense fighting in the streets of Travnik. My own car was hit several times. And later that day, we were evacuated by British forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were able or unable to make contact with the joint command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no contact possible with the joint command. We had our own radio means to call BritBat for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that same day, the 4th of June, did you go to both Busovaca and Vitez, discovering a new argument arising with the HVO in Busovaca, who refused altogether to negotiate with the ABiH commanding officer on the ground that this officer was too junior to make important decisions such as those about ceasefires?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The HVO side in Busovaca claims that Mr. Mekic, whom we had been speaking with during all the previous meetings, was no longer the right person to talk with, since he had no mandate, according to the HVO. And the same thing happened in Vitez, where they claimed that Sifet Sivro, commander of the brigade, ABiH, the 325 Mountain Brigade, was no longer a partner in the discussions since he had no mandate as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, once again in this testimony, I should like to seize the opportunity to tell you that you need to focus on things that are, indeed, pertinent from the point of view of the case before us. I believe that all this context, all the details, everything that happened in that region, need not really be all that pertinent to the case before us. All these events need to be related to the case before us, because as you know, we do have the problem of time. We have a very tight schedule, and I do beg you to bear it always in mind, and we need to finish the testimony of this witness by the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two points, or three. First, I suspect that a full history of events will be of value to the Tribunal. Second, the judgement that I and my team make on what is material is reflected in the document, and matters that are not contentious occupy very little time indeed, but the full matrix for you to consider will be made available. Third, if and where, by prereading the document, the Chamber is quite sure that material is not required, we can, of course, eliminate it. As it is, the last few paragraphs, I think, have taken just a few minutes of your time but have flushed out the picture very fully, and I hope that this presentation will ultimately be shown to be of value to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can I follow that? This is entirely with respect to the witness, of course, who has come here at considerable inconvenience, no doubt, to tell us about his experiences. The question really is whether we are assisted by this degree of detail about precisely everything that happened in the Lasva Valley during the time. Now, the Prosecution are initially in the best position to judge that. We would be grateful if you would consider whether we actually need all this detail as time goes by.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll do our best to make it ever briefer. What one can't ever forecast with precision is where events, for example, events of non-cooperation, will fit in at the end with a picture and a more detailed picture of the individual defendant's involvement, and that's why that matrix may be of value. But, of course, I'm only too glad to eliminate matters that the Chamber feels or is satisfied are unlikely to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that would be helpful. I'm going to have to announce a few hearings in November. There's another case which the Trial Chamber has got to deal with, and it's going to take some afternoons. But I'll deal with that in due course. But again, that has a bearing on what we've been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could take this matter fairly rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 5th of June, there were the two shells that -- or two shells fell on Zenica. The local commission had the usual complaints of ceasefire, with counter-allegations by the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mistreatment of Croats in Zenica was alleged. Following that, on the 6th of June, there was a meeting with Jozic at the HVO Brigade headquarters in Vitez; the blockade in Kruscica still in place; the HVO requesting the evacuation of 10.000 Croats from Guca Gora; BritBat announcing the HVO were withdrawing from Travnik and, "We're going to burn the archives"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 7th of June, I think you managed to get into Travnik via the help of BritBat. You found 130 wounded men in the hospital. There was an evacuation of one wounded man and some women agreed upon, but that failed because the HVO checkpoint at Dolac was unable to cooperate or declined to cooperate?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were 13 wounded selected by the doctor, male and female from all kinds of origin, so Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document 1024, which I can deal with, I think, very briefly to identify this. It's a report of the 7th of June and it's at page 5, paragraph 20. I think that's the only paragraph or possibly one other. 5th of June, Kiseljak reported the area of Novi Travnik, T-junction shelled, and then an account of the injuries and the account of a humanitarian convoy being targeted. And if you go over several pages to paragraph 60 on page 11 for a highlight. Kiseljak reporting intimidation against remaining Muslim families in Vitez and surrounding villages. Conducted allegation of Jokeri perpetration. I think you know about these Jokers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document, and I am going to go as fast as we can now, for general speed, because the documents can speak for themselves and be incorporated in closing argument documents wherever appropriate. But this is another document dated the 7th of June. If we could look at Zenica, at page 9, a note that it's dealt with -- various Zenica matters are dealt with on page 9 and onwards. We will incorporate this in closing arguments and the defence will notice that it exists. Can we move to the 8th of June. And this is something I have to deal with other than by leading, but nevertheless I'll set the scene. Did you receive reports on the 8th of June about fighting in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the state of the HVO headquarters? What was being complained of?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by BritBat and by my own hearing. I heard the explosions, that there was fighting going on in the area of Guca Gora. And we went to the operational zone headquarters in Vitez, the HVO headquarters, to get extra information. And the soldiers at the door and the officers inside the headquarters seemed more or less in panic. They begged us for help to save their people. And explained to us that large atrocities were going on in the area of Guca Gora, that the old Catholic church in Guca Gora was in flames, and that thousands of people were fleeing towards Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Guca Gora, incidentally, can be seen on the map we were looking at yesterday on the top left-hand corner. This map here. If you just simply place it on the ELMO. Did you meet the man Alagic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Travnik to meet Alagic and the responsible commander at the ABiH site.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was he able to help you with?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was able to escort us to Guca Gora itself, and he suggested to bring a Catholic priest from Travnik with us. And with the help of the British Battalion we went to Guca Gora that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was your intelligence about what the HVO were doing at this area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that the HVO was withdrawing from Guca Gora or already had withdrawn from Guca Gora. And HVO told us that there was a lot of fighting going on and a lot of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was happening so far as the crossing of lines was concerned, and the HVO soldiers crossing lines to VRS?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that same meeting with Alagic, we were told by Mr. Alagic himself that the front lines towards the Serbs, the HVO positions had been handed over. A large part of the HVO soldiers, together with Croat civilians, fled to the Serb side. And that the ABiH had been able to close the front line again and to take over the old HVO positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have intelligence as to what was happening to HVO soldiers who declined to cross those lines?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them refused. Quite a large group stayed with the ABiH and fought together with them against the Serbs. And some of the soldiers were threatened and killed because they refused to cross the lines. British reconnaissance cleared that situation and found a lot of left behind luggage and civilian cars and weapons on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 95. Colonel Alagic went with you to Guca Gora, we've just dealt with that, to prove that what was being said by the HVO was rumours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We saw ourselves the church in Guca Gora. There were no HVO soldiers in Guca Gora. There was no visible damage in Guca Gora. The church was intact, and approximately 200 civilians were hiding in the church, and UNHCR was already present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found one injured man. When the British soldiers searched the streets of Guca Gora, they found one man killed, shot through the head. And this injured man inside the church, we treated the man and brought him to Nova Bila Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The international press, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The press did not come with us. They broadcasted the news from the point of view of the Croats during the evening, international press. They broadcasted that the old church of Guca Gora was in flames, and that many hundreds of Croats had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at some photographs very briefly to show what you were able to find and show the falsity of what was being said. 1835 is one of the photographs in the pack. That's that one. And it's the following photographs, 1836 and 2123. This photograph shows --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows one of the British vehicles, a British liaison officer, and an interpreter, my colleague monitor, and our interpreter, and on the left-hand side the Catholic priest from Travnik coming with us to see with his own eyes what actually was true and what was untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next photograph, 1836. The church said to have been --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the old church in Guca Gora, the Catholic church. It's still intact. Nothing damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then 2123.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a view from the front side of the church in the southern direction, and within the circle you can see smoke coming from a Muslim village, set ablaze as a revenge for the allegations in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the name of that village is?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bandol.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning to the documentary exhibits. Could you just again record 1031 as the next document. You set out these allegations -- this history on the first page, I think.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first page, it's the introduction by Mr. Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the second and third page are written about Mr. Watters and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They set out in detail the summary you've given, and again it will be available for analysis at a later stage. There should also be 103,1 there as well. I trust the Chamber has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the Chamber has understood that there were unfounded rumours. I think, Mr. Nice, you can go forward now, at least so far as the proceedings now are concerned. If you wish to come back to that, perhaps later on, you can always come back to that. We have the document and we know now that there were rumours that had no foundation. I think we can cover all this very, very quickly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 9th of June there is another passage that I am not in a position to lead, so I shall. Did you make a further visit to Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We met with the representatives, the UNHCR, the night before, and made a plan together with the British Battalion to evacuate the 200 people, the Croat people in the Guca Gora church. And with the help of BritBat we managed to bring these people to the Nova Bila Hospital. They didn't need treatment in the hospital, but that was the most common place to bring them to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you reach an agreement with Merdan?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Merdan being from the 3rd Corps army ABiH, gave us permission to organise this, and with help of Alagic, being the commander on scene, we were able to cross the lines. And we had some problems at a Muslim checkpoint, but we finally solved that problem and after a few hours we were able to evacuate those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In light of what Judge Bennouna has said, can I just deal with this in this way. Was it false propaganda that lead to Croats fleeing towards Vitez and Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can read the next five paragraphs, but there are some documents to look at. At that time did you also meet the HVO commander, a man who threatened to kill you if you ever went to Kruscica again?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was at the same Nova Bila hospital when we brought in the 200 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this man -- 2533 is the photograph we looked at yesterday. This is the man you described as the red-faced man?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know who his commander was?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe his commander was Mr. Cerkez, since he accompanied Mr. Cerkez during the first meeting where all his battalion commanders were available, were present.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you ask the witness and counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 10th of June did you go to Visiko and Split, or via Visiko to Split, and discover a lot of fighting in Kakanj and the Vares area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's set out at documents 1040 and 1041, which I think we are going to take as read for these purposes. Oh, yes. It sets out -- deals with the Convoy of Joy, but I think the Chamber is now well familiar with that. So we can just deal with -- leave the document in. On the 17th of June -- yes, I think I've included 1040 and 1041. On the 17th of June, Colonel, were you briefed that no evidence could be found of massacres or of mass destruction, but that a lot of houses had been robbed, and that in Kakanj a lot of Croats had fled to the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was in relation to allegations made of what?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same allegations as in the Guca Gora area, that there were large atrocities being done against the Croat community, and there were large threats, and that's the reason why people fled to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 18th of June, did you visit Vitez, there being no changes in the front -- right. I'm so sorry. I am going too fast. I am trying to listen to the French translation to see when the questions end, in order not to disturb the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, to finish this question of propaganda, false propaganda. Propaganda is always a bit false, but regarding this business of propaganda, does the Colonel know why, according to him, the HVO resorted to this propaganda to make Croats flee towards the Serb lines? What was the motivation, in your opinion, Colonel? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this very often, Your Honour, in the ECMM headquarters with Mr. Thebault and the other monitors. And my belief and our belief is that they were interested in certain areas, and that's the reason why they pulled all the Croats from outside into those areas and they were not interested in other areas. So they more or less gave them up and tried to save the lives of the Croats living in those areas. And by making a deal with the Bosnian Serb side, a deal of safe passage, maybe for money or weapons, they could save the lives from people living in areas they were not interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sir, I think in the terminology of the area, there is ethnic cleansing and there is also reverse ethnic cleansing. Is that a terminology with which you are familiar?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never used that terminology, but I understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And does that terminology fit with the answers you've just given to the judge?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 100. On the 18th of June, Colonel, did you visit Vitez, no changes in the front lines had occurred, but neither side had respected the ceasefire. Soldiers killed every day. About 11.000, mainly Croat refugees by now arrived at Vitez, of whom 4.000 stayed. The rest going to Busovaca and Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Still no access to Kruscica and on the 19th of June, I mustn't lead, did you meet Grubesic from the HVO in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He said -- what did he say by way of --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were claims about civilians being forced to dig trenches, again in the same village of Skradno, and he didn't deny it. He more or less agreed. And he explained that a lot of his soldiers had been killed the night before, and that angry civilians, may be relatives of those soldiers, forced civilians from the other side, civilians from Skradno, to dig the trenches. He, by then, was aware of the fact that this was a -- against the Geneva Convention, since I told him several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is dealt with in various reports. 1073,1, again it may be the Busovaca entry where you record, and just before the middle of the page, "HVO reported specific --" is that it, or special orders?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Special orders -- I don't see the difference between specific or special.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. "On new ceasefire agreement. Calm today. Not aware that forcing civilians to dig trenches is regarded as a war crime."

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's the point of view of the HVO. I'm sure that they must be aware, since I told them more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1084,1, a document of your own. You deal again under paragraph 5 with rumours and with confidence building. Over the page, five lines down, "The HVO brigade commander admitted that civilians were forced to dig trenches, but stated the BiH did the same, and stated that his people were very bitter because of soldiers killed, promising to stop the violation of the Geneva Convention." The photographs to look at are 1711, which is a picture of a man in a beret. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's the HVO brigade commander in Busovaca, Mr. Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whom you were speaking?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The map we've already looked at. Paragraph 103, which I can read. On that same day, the 9th of June, did you go to Rankovici, a mainly Croat village close to Novi Travnik, where five trucks missing from the Convoy of Joy were found, only one intact, the rest having been robbed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 20th of June did you go to investigate the allegation of a massacre and of HVO prisoners in Senkovici?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A predominantly Muslim area, finding no evidence of a massacre, Croats gathered in five houses there, the women and children were free to move. The local commander explaining that the HVO had abandoned the place?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This being set out in the next written document, 1085. Various paragraphs refer and you make reference to the trucks and so on. But the document can speak for itself, unless Mr. Scott draws to my attention anything that absolutely requires our valuable time now. Yes. Perhaps it's worth seeing. Just towards the foot of the page, beside, "VOPP" Vance-Owen Plan. A record of the HVO being glad that the plan was dead. Can you explain that at all?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also a discussion that happened that last few days several times during all kinds of meetings with HVO, and they explained to us that they never believed in the plan and they were glad it was finally dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 105. On the 21st of June, did you try to get again to Senkovici, coming under Serb fire?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Eventually, five weeks after your first attempt and with UNHCR support, getting to Kruscica to deliver aid?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the civilian roadblock still in place, and you used the secondary road, opened on the order of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this a road the existence of which you had earlier not known of?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that there was anything that actually would have stopped your using this road throughout the five-week period, had you been informed of its existence?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. According to my opinion, we could have used that road any day if there was any help from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your concern, over the five-week period, had been to get much-needed humanitarian aid into this village?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We pleaded for that several times, nearly every day. And I tried to force myself through the roadblock several times, but I never managed it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 106, I must not lead. Were you aware of a fax sent by Mate Boban to Morillon on the 22nd of June?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed of that by the ambassador, Mr. Thebault, during one of our meetings in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of the content of that fax?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't fully recall it, but the contents were again about atrocities being done against Croats and Mr. Boban asking Mr. Morillon to save his people and to help the Croats finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did this make reference to Catholic sacred objects?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He also spoke about or wrote in his fax about allegations that the holy Catholic places like churches were being damaged by the ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In reality, what was the position so far as Catholic churches and mosques and minarets is concerned?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We hardly at any -- found any damage on Catholic churches so far, and we checked a lot of them, and there was a lot of damage on the minarets and mosques on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The attitude of the clerics? Catholic priests, for example.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found some of the priests very helpful, like Father Stjepan from Zenica. Some of the others were fairly radical in their thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were they free to practice their religion and move in areas otherwise dominated by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were, almost all of them, free to practice their masses and Catholic beliefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the other hand, in Busovaca, what was the position of the imam there?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was certainly not free to move, and he was not able to do his services.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 108, I must not lead. On the 23rd of June, did you go to collect your interpreter from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's my interpreter, Marijana, a Croat interpreter. She lived near Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did she, first of all, tell you what had happened so far as Muslims in Kiseljak were concerned?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She told me that the days before, all remaining Muslims had been forced out of the area of Kiseljak, and she also told me that she heard a radio broadcast that all Croats should be prepared and -- pack their luggage and belongings and be prepared to flee to Ilidza. Ilidza is close to Sarajevo, in Serb hands. He also stated on that same radio broadcast, according to my interpreter, that Mr. Kordic was no longer allowed to negotiate with the ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from my interpreter, Marijana, and she told me that Mr. Boban said this in a radio broadcast. I had to rely on my interpreter, as I did for three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The place to which the evacuating Croats would have to go was where?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A place called Ilidza, and that's a place near Sarajevo. At that time, Ilidza was in Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you try to meet the local joint commission of Kacuni, but did the HVO not show up?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can read right down to paragraph 116, and I shall do so swiftly. Shuttle diplomacy on the 24th of June. On the 25th of June -- I'm sorry, I should have produced Exhibit 1102,1, which I now do. That records what you've just been telling us about Muslims being ordered to leave Kiseljak. That's in the first paragraph. Thank you. So the 25th of June, you were working on the evacuation of patients from Nova Bila hospital, meeting local commanders in Kacuni, and the HVO still holding a number of soldiers and civilians. That's dealt with in the next document, 1122, page 8. Thank you very much. It may be that this will help the Court. Under the "Travnik" entry: "Attended a meeting of senior Croat political representatives from Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik, and Busovaca. The meeting was used as an opportunity to question ECMM policy on population moves from Travnik to Zenica. The meeting was informed that ECMM would not be involved, and a lively debate followed. When asked if the HVO/HDZ interest in such moves was the pursuit of a political policy, this was denied. When it was stated by --" Who is that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Head of CC Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. "... representatives from Travnik and Guca Gora had made enquires about returning, he was informed that this was not appropriate and care should be taken about who ECMM talked to. The attempt to silence any alternative view has insidious overtones, and HCC was pleased to inform the meeting that the ECMM would seek the views of those they chose." Colonel, how does this fit in with the question Judge Bennouna asked you earlier and the answer you gave?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It gives a clear summary of my point of view, that they asked us to check allegations again and again, and if we gave them the answers of our findings, then they say, "Well, you have to look at another place. You probably didn't look proper or didn't find the right place or didn't look at the right place."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. 26th of June, evacuation of 24 patients from Travnik; one group to Nova Bila, one to Vitez, and a third to Kruscica. The 28th of June, a meeting of the provincial government of Travnik --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was the first day that we really were able to break the human blockade in Kruscica, since we had to bring cured patients to Nova Bila and to Kruscica. One of the doctors from Nova Bila assisted us, and he was able to convince the civilians at the roadblock to step aside and to let us through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 28th of June, meeting of the provincial government of Travnik, with Muslim and Croat representatives. Muslims refused to speak to the HVO. You were mediating. The commander of 308 Brigade in Novi Travnik told you of capturing tanks and howitzers, guns, and anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document Z1129, please. This is a list, essentially, of killed and missing. Can you help with this, please?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a list I got from Mr. Skopljak. The first page is a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second page is his introduction, and then there's the list itself. He handed me this list at the 29th of June, or it was supplied the 29th of June, consisting of missing, dead, and imprisoned Croat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able, in due course, to check the accuracy or otherwise of this list?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The normal procedure was to hand a list like this over to the ICRC in Zenica, and they would take care of finding missing people, and organising the exchange of imprisoned people, and, if possible, finding the dead people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 114. On the 30th of June, an attempt to revive the joint commission in Vitez; ABiH side cancelled because they had too much to do in Zepce; Nakic told you that the ABiH had attacked the HVO from three sides and that the HVO, with 40.000 refugees, had been forced to flee to VRS territory; the ABiH told you later that in reality the HVO was cooperating with the VRS in the area and that they had deliberately withdrawn in order to give room to VRS to move in?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document 1132, page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Nice. What the colonel has just said, and I'm addressing myself to the witness, does this come from the same motivation that he gave us a moment ago, and that is the withdrawal of a population towards a territory of interest to the HVO, while seeding another less-interesting part to someone else which one could describe as a fresh occupation of territory by the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my opinion, Your Honour, Zepce, north of Zenica, was a small enclave which the HVO could not hold for a long time. I think that they were not interested in Zepce at all, so they withdrew all the people from Zepce to a safe area for them, being Serb-held territory, and then travel through safe area maybe towards Croatia or towards another part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your opinion, Colonel, was there an agreement between the HVO and VRS regarding these movements?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw an agreement myself, but I'm sure that there was a local -- at least a local agreement to give people safe passage. If not, in a war situation with two armies opposite each other in a front line, you can never cross this line with a whole unit and with thousands of civilians without any casualties, so there must be an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Picking up on Judge Bennouna's concerns and questions, I think -- I don't know that I need take you back to it, but in one of your earlier documents, that is, 1122, for the 28th of June in relation to Zenica, did you say that there was testimony on Muslim ethnic cleansing in Central Bosnia -- it's page 9 -- evidence that there is some HVO policy to move Croats to major Croat centres, and in the south there is growing tension against the Muslims? Did you say that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But following on from the question that you've just been asked, any collusion or agreement between the HVO and the Serbs, what significance would that have for HVO resources and their availability for use against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO forces withdraw from the area of Travnik were sighted later on in the area of Bugojno and further south, so they were able to use these forces again. I don't know whether they had to hand in the weapons, but there wasn't a shortage of small arms, so they could use the soldiers themselves again on other front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, self-evidently, if there was collaboration between the HVO and the Serbs, it becomes two to one as against the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They gave the ABiH side a hard time regaining the lost ground when HVO troops gave themselves in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 115. Was it your judgement at that time that the Serbs had little remaining interest in claiming Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no sign of Serbs attacking HVO positions at the front lines any more. Most of the times, they attacked the ABiH positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 1st of July, did you hear of heavy fighting all over the Lasva Valley, and did you make a round trip of different hospitals in Busovaca and Travnik, noting that in Croat-led hospitals, there was better equipment?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the patients in the Busovaca hospital were all Croats, whereas the patients in the ABiH-controlled hospital in Travnik were more mixed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's dealt with in document 1132,1, which I produce but I don't think we need focus on. Paragraph 117, I must not lead. Did you, on the 2nd of July, go to Busovaca in relation to drivers of trucks belonging to Medecins du Monde and Medecins sans Frontieres?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was informed by telephone, by representative of Medecins du Monde, that four trucks with goods belonging to them were taken off the road in Busovaca by HVO soldiers. The next morning, I picked up one of the male representatives of Medecins du Monde, and we tried to go to Busovaca. But the road was blocked, the Lasva road we normally use, so it took us a long time to get to Busovaca. We spoke to the chief of police, Mr. Ljubesic, and in the beginning he agreed in releasing the four truck drivers. But we claimed that we also wanted the trucks and the cargo back, since it was international cargo meant for supplies -- UNHCR supplies in Zenica and for some specific hospitals, donated by the western countries. He told us, this chief of police, that he needed let's say the green light from the chief of police in Mostar, so he was not able to decide, himself. We tried to find Mr. Grubesic, the brigade commander of the HVO. He was not available for us, and we were told that we had to come back the next day and then we would get drivers and trucks and cargo back. So the 3rd of July, we went to Busovaca again. The roadblock was still there. With the assistance of British Battalion, two Warrior vehicles, we tried to make our way to the location where the trucks were. We found the drivers in good shape, but the HVO soldiers were already unloading the trucks. We protested against that. Then these soldiers threatened me with their weapons. They threatened to kill me and my interpreter if we wouldn't leave within 15 minutes and take just the drivers with us. We refused. With the help of BritBat, we finally managed to get the drivers and the trucks, but we lost the cargo. We made a large protest at the brigade headquarters. Mr. Grubesic, the chief of police, was no longer available, and finally we returned with drivers and empty trucks to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One last question on that topic. On the second visit, the 3rd of July, what did Grubesic say about authority he needed to release the trucks?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he needed authority from his commanding officer, being Mr. Blaskic in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he indicate whether he got it or not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, whether he had permission or not. Finally, we got trucks and drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two documents that deal with this are 1136,1 and 1138. I think they cover the territory, and I produce them, or the witness does. I can now read right the way down to 121, and that's to say right up until any other conclusions of the witness. Paragraph 118. Throughout your tenure, did you see special forces in the area, especially close to the village of Nadioci? In a restaurant in that village, nearly every day were there well-armed men in black uniforms who you judged to be extremists, well armed, and seen by you at various front lines and in Vitez? Did they also have an HVO truck with a three-barrel anti-aircraft gun mounted on it and a buffalo horn or something similar on the front, and is that a truck you had also seen in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you also see individual soldiers from time to time wearing uniforms with HV insignias; you once asked a man about such a uniform, and he replied that uniforms were hard to obtain so he had simply taken one with the HV insignia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you also once see a tank which may have come from Croatia, and did you once see an HV helicopter landing in the area, being informed of other sightings of helicopters at the ammunitions factory in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the tank was more an anti-aircraft gun, a double-barrelled heavy gun. A ZFU 54-2, I guess it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1139,1 would be the next exhibit. I'm not sure that we need trouble with it, actually. It's one of your documents. We'll produce it, please, 1139,1. Paragraph 120. Did you form the view that the ABiH in general was poorly or badly uniformed, many of them wearing civilian or part-civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were they less well armed with less-sophisticated equipment than the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Mr. Nice, I should like to go back to the paragraph 119. The witness saw the HV helicopters, if I understood him properly, or did he hear those helicopters? Could you be more precise regarding the fact of helicopters belonging to HV in that region? Did you see them or hear them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... heard one or saw others, but I'll ask the witness to give his own unled reply.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I saw one HIP-type helicopter landing at the ammunition factory site west of Vitez. I heard several helicopters during other occasions, and I heard from my colleague ECMM monitors that they sometimes saw a helicopter as well. So I only sighted one myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you saw yourself one HV helicopter that is belonging to the Croatian army and you heard from other ECMM colleagues that it was quite a common sight to see these helicopters land next to the ammunitions factories in Vitez; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't told by other monitors that the place where they landed was a common sight. It struck me why an HV helicopter or a Croatian helicopter should land at an ammunition factory site near Vitez. I couldn't find no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said you actually heard the sound of helicopters yourself; is that right? Or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw one helicopter myself landing there. I heard on other occasions helicopters, but I didn't see them at that occasion. And the third part is that my colleague monitors told me that they already had seen helicopters before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sticking with the second -- sticking with the second point. You physically heard helicopters. Did you ever see helicopters in the area bearing HVO insignia to account for the noise of the helicopters you actually heard?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was informed by the intelligence of the British Battalion that the HVO had no helicopters of their own in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have any helicopters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 121. Did you ever receive investigation reports from the HVO following the matters of one kind or another that were complained of; Ahmici, the truck bomb, the Zenica shelling?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never did receive any reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In light of your experience and expertise, what view, if any, did you form about the pattern of attacks on Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my opinion, formed during my period in Bosnia, the tactics the HVO used were to define what areas were of interest. Those areas they wanted to keep should be cleansed of all Muslim inhabitants, and they used the tactic of fear; by shooting at houses during the night; by setting houses on fire; by scaring away the people, first by killing some of them and then scaring the rest away; by putting, if possible, a lot of people into gaol and using them as a bargain to free people from the other side. In the areas where they did not have any interest, they would scare their own people by broadcasting and by using their own officers in the area to force the people to leave that territory and to go either to the Lasva Valley or go to other Croat areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second, from your knowledge of the command structure of the HVO, and from your knowledge of military structures generally, do you have an opinion about the potential of a military police unit to operate within or outside central control and command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my acknowledged military police units, the name itself states that already military police always operate within the military structure. They have a clear hierarchy, and most of the times the commander on scene, being the operational zone commander, gives orders to the military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see anything to indicate that it was possible for any such military police unit here to operate outside those standard chains of command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only sign I got was the excuse given by the chief of police in Busovaca, the chief of military police, Mr. Ljubesic, that he couldn't deal with these four trucks and drivers himself on that 2nd of July, but that he needed allowance from his chief in Mostar. And that would mean a second line of command next to the operational zone command in the area of Busovaca-Vitez. So it didn't make any sense that military police in Busovaca were not expecting orders from their own area, being Mr. Blaskic in Vitez, but he had to rely on orders coming from Mostar. That, in my point of view, would be an unworkable situation for military police. So I just thought that this was an excuse for him not to release these four drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think 124 has now been covered. The last two documents, 1140,1, please. Under Vitez. Just a matter of detail, sad detail. On the 6th of July an interpreter working for BritBat was killed by a sniper. She, in civilian clothes, talking with British soldiers in front of a U.N. occupied house within the perimeter of the BritBat camp. The shot coming from a house showing an HVO flag, in an HVO controlled area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Over the page, please. Paragraph 4. To pick up the earlier questions. Other matters reported. "Guards at the echelon in Vitez have sighted a MI 8 HIP --" you may have to explain that -- "helicopter."

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "HIP" is the native code name for this type of helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Landing at the ammunition factory and then taking off in the direction of Travnik. Then at the end of this block, paragraph 4. Intelligence coming your way about Cerkez. Can you just tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Repeat that again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of paragraph 4, on the second sheet, HVO is giving rewards.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed by BritBat again, since under 4 it says BritBat reported that, that the HVO was giving rewards for parts of human bodies, like ears and fingers. And this order came from Mr. Cerkez. They told us that one cut off ear already was found on an HVO prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last document of this type, 1140,2. I think this is simply your farewell. And it records the end of your time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've covered all the exhibits, bar a few, the photograph exhibits. And for completeness, I'll deal with that. Your Honour, just give me a minute. Alternatively, it may be that in my anxiety to deal with things quickly I've dealt with something too quickly, and Mr. Scott's judgement is preferable to mine on this. It's only one topic. I don't know if we are going to take a break about now. What would be left would be a few minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you can have a few minutes, but a few minutes, because we want to finish the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know who is going to cross-examine. Mr. Sayers, you will not be criticised if you don't go over this matter in detail, the detail which has been gone through. You've heard what the Chamber said about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I truly appreciate that, and I think that it might be appropriate for the Trial Chamber to urge us to move on, if it feels that we are driving a point into the ground, since we are much closer to it than the Trial Chamber is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, we'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a few more minutes. The other topic that I want to ask the witness about is the Convoy of Joy. You will recall that I said, when I touched on it in one of his documents, that we heard a lot about it already, but Mr. Scott and Ms. Verhaag remind me, hopefully, that there has been objection to the degree of hearsay in the information coming about the Convoy of Joy so far, although the evidence has been admitted. So if I can just ask the witness just briefly what his degree of contact, if any, was with it. That may help the Chamber. And then I'll deal with the few remaining photographs and I'll be finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, did you have any dealings with the Convoy of Joy yourself?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. During the preparation phase, especially the community of Travnik asked us to support this Convoy of Joy, mainly coming from the area of Tuzla, heading for the coast, to load all kinds of goods, most of them food. Then heading back for Tuzla, but also heading back for Travnik and other places. I think there was a total, up to about 300 or 400 trucks of all kinds, and they asked the ECMM and the British Battalion to escort this Convoy of Joy. I don't know the reason, but in the end it was rejected by BritBat. I think due to lack of enough vehicles to be able to escort it. They asked us to mediate, to lead this convoy through all kinds of checkpoints. My team was only able to mediate in the area of the Lasva Valley, of course. And during the return of the convoy I was on leave a few days. When I came back from that leave, I found some of the trucks in Rankovici near Novi Travnik. We found some other trucks in Busovaca, some of them in Vitez, some of them in Nova Bila. And I was told by my fellow monitor, who stayed during my period on leave, what happened to this convoy in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there. The trucks in Rankovici, Novi Travnik and Busovaca and Vitez, by whom had they been hijacked?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment I found them, they were in HVO controlled area. I didn't see them being hijacked myself, but I guess it must have been done within that same territory under control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were told things by your fellow monitors. Was any of them an eyewitness to any part of the stopping of the convoy itself?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether they saw it with their own eyes. But my Greek fellow monitor Mr. Stauros Kinigopoulos, and British monitor Phillip Watkins, they were present during that day and night when the convoy entered the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are either of those going to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No -- well, one might. But, at most, one might. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, obviously, we would object on the grounds of double hearsay, and we don't even know whether the persons to whom the Colonel spoke were actually eyewitnesses, and I believe he just testified that he doesn't either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's hear what the reports were and then we'll decide whether to admit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the reports I heard from Mr. Watkins and Mr. Kinigopoulos were that when this Convoy of Joy, approximately 300 loaded trucks, loaded with food and fuel and all kinds of things, entered the HVO controlled territory in Novi Travnik, and then entered the Lasva Valley, this convoy was more or less split into separate small parts of 10 or maybe 15 vehicles. And these groups of vehicles were threatened by civilians, local soldiers watching. Some of the truck drivers, I think a total of 10, had been killed, or executed, as my fellow monitors told me. And the goods from the trucks had been looted by the local civilians and brought to private houses and to warehouses. Some of the trucks, as in evidence we found later on, especially in Rankovici, but also individual trucks in the area of Vitez and Nova Bila and Busovaca, and these trucks were clearly damaged by -- the windows were smashed, windows of some of the vehicles, and all vehicles were empty and all the goods were gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made a summary of this in the documents we've already seen?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There remains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's in documents 1040 and 1041, and in particular he makes reference there to the killings of the truck drivers, although I think he numbers them as 8 at that stage, but it may be he adds the other two.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There might be one thing I have to add. There is one truck, specific truck, near the Catholic church in Rankovici that was not damaged and all the goods were still in that truck. I was told by the priest that he was able to save this truck from being hijacked, and this truck was meant to go to a community near Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just now conclude the exhibits you've produced? That will just take a minute, with the usher's assistance. Just a couple of maps. There's one A4 map that just is out of turn, but just explain it to us. It's Z1172. Just tell us what that was or is, as you've drawn it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map shows you Vitez and the road along the Lasva River, and the small circle on the right-hand side shows the village of Strane, and south of that, the village of Skradno. Skradno was the village where the people complained about being forced to dig trenches, and Strane, the encircled area, is the place where I saw this HVO man, Mr. Marinac, and the civilians carrying shovels, having a porch, and I'm convinced that these people were busy digging trenches at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. 1690, on which you've drawn -- it's a helpful aerial view of the T-junction and Kaonik and so on, but you've drawn a red line and a white circle?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This aerial photograph was shown to me during my testimony in the Blaskic case. I was asked what routes I took from my visit to Jelinak on my way to Strane and Skradno, so I appointed this route in orange on this aerial photograph. The encircled part is the -- are the aerial photographs of trenches in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In your photograph album -- or not photograph album -- in the extracts from your photograph album, there are just a few that need explanation. First of all, the first sheet.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The central photograph is the house, the ECMM house we used next to the BritBat camp in Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which we can see above?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the top photograph is part of the British camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next sheet?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, on the top photo, you see the bridge across the Lasva River in the eastern part of Vitez. This bridge was blocked by a kind of tractor. There were mines on the road, and there was a sign on this tractor warning us for mines. So there was no freedom of movement for UNPROFOR or for ECMM at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that a typical sort of roadblock or not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specific roadblock was removed after approximately two weeks, and several vehicles were more than once used for the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Five sheets on, there's a photograph which has, in the top left-hand corner, an extract of a map marked by you. The Chamber will want to be aware that the map it asked us to prepare is in an advanced state of preparation as to front lines. But did you, in fact, from time to time mark front lines yourself, hand drawing them on maps --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- to reflect the position?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was important for our own safety to know exactly where front lines were, since we were not allowed to go to the front lines themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other picture on that page, just tell us about that, the two pictures.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The top picture shows General Halilovic just after the meeting, I think, of the 29th of April, where both parties agreed on a ceasefire and where we stressed both commanders to visit the troops on the front line, to tell the soldiers themselves that they agreed on the ceasefire. This part of that visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just finally just something I should have showed earlier, two sheets on and two sheets altogether, the first marked the 9th of May. Just about these, please.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is early in the period in Kruscica, when Kruscica was still open. At that picture, you see one of the ambulances of the British Battalion preparing to bring a wounded Croat civilian to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next sheet, please, and is this the old man you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, that's the old man I spoke of, the man we evacuated to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That concludes my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, my name is Steve Sayers. I represent Dario Kordic, along with my colleague here, Mr. Naumovski. We have a wide amount of territory to cover, so if you can answer the question in as short a manner as possible, maybe that will assist us in our mutual goal of getting your testimony completed as early as possible. Just a few matters of preliminary detail which the Court may or may not already be aware of. First, it would be fair to say that you are a professional soldier in the Dutch armed forces and that you have been in the armed forces since 1976; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you have 23 years of experience in the military?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
