utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the document also states on page 6 that reports had been received of a new formation, the Muslim forces army, which only accepts Islamic soldiers from Bosnia and abroad, but is assessed to be under 2.000 strong. Was that subject ever raised during the briefing that you received, sir?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that briefing I already got some information that a unit of that kind was being formed, and I think that it's approximately the same amount of soldiers I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about the 7th Muslim brigade actually being the principal source of tensions in areas where offensive operations were being conducted by the forces of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During nearly every meeting in Busovaca we got allegations from the HVO side of small attacks, so I wouldn't call it offensive operations, but small attacks or incidents at the front lines, and more than once the HVO side claimed that Mujahedins or Mujahedin forces were active at those front lines. And similar claims were made during the commissions in Vitez. So I was informed by one side about allegations on Mujahedins being involved in this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever receive information from the officers in the British intelligence cells that that, in fact, was the case, the 7th Muslim brigade was the principal source of tension in areas where fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that the British officers stated that the cause of the problems were these Mujahedins. I only recall one incident, but I don't know whether it is defined as such. That's the incident of the killing of four or five Croat men, young men. Some were in a small village north of Guca Gora, some 10 kilometres north, where they were said to be a training camp of Mujahedins soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber has already heard evidence about that. That was the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. I couldn't remember the name, and that's correct. I was informed about that incident, I think, by the British. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to close the door on that particular subject. You don't have any personal knowledge of what went on in that village? Your knowledge is derived from what you were told?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I wrote down the names to check it, but I couldn't find any way to positively identify this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read you a very brief extract from the Cheshire Regiment's milinfosum number 148 on the 27th of March, 1993, dealing with Kakanj. It says: "The main source of tension in the area is the presence and attitude of MOS --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- were you aware of the 7th Muslim brigade actually conducting operations in the Kakanj area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. But that was long before I arrived in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You were in the area, though, on the 23rd of June of 1993, right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And at that time, I believe, there had been a changeover in the identity of the British regiment that constituted the BritBat component of UNPROFOR; the Cheshire Regiment had been replaced by the Prince of Wales Own Regiment?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read you an entry from the Prince of Wales Own Regiment, milinfosum 55 on the 23rd of June, 1993. I would like to ask you if this is consistent with your experience. It regards an incident in Zenica. It says: "The ECMM report another incident that Mujahedins elements in Zenica attacking a woman for wearing clothes that were inappropriate. This attack is reputedly only one in a series where the victims are beaten or even knifed. The Zenica LO, liaison officer, also noted that Mujahedin members were seen entering the ops room at the 3rd Corps HQ." And the comment goes on to say: "Whether the Mujahedin are under effective control of the 3rd Corps or not, has been a topic of some debate. This cell believes that they under effective control, as they are invariably found at the point of the 3rd Corps main effort. The recent campaign in the Bila valley clearly demonstrated this. However, the Mujahedin are clearly capable of extreme acts, as demonstrated by the attacks in Zenica and the desecration of the church in Guca Gora." On that subject, sir, are you aware that the building just as you come into the monastery had been shelled repeatedly?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What building are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The large square building just before you get into the monastery at Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Guca Gora, at the 23rd of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I visited this church more than once. That was, as I recall it, on the 9th and, I think, on the 8th of June. And my fellow monitor, Mr. Watkins, visited the area north of Guca Gora in the days after, in the period when I was on leave. So I don't think -- or I didn't write anything down on Guca Gora after, I think, the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The intelligence cell goes on to make an observation that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I just wonder how this is going to help us. You can refer to all those documents, Mr. Sayers, in due course. This witness has given his evidence. He, as far as I know, has not seen any of these documents. Now, his evidence is, for instance, that he saw little damage to churches but much to mosques. If you want to challenge that, then as far as the witness is concerned, you can simply do it globally by putting that there was damage to the place that you've mentioned or any others. You don't have to read out all these documents all the time, which take up a lot of our time, and it's not terribly helpful when the witness hasn't seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that that's a helpful suggestion, and I will abide by it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Globally speaking, before you left Central Bosnia-Herzegovina in, I believe it was, the second week of July --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- had you visited, for example, the church in Guca Gora since the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe on the 9th of June was the latest day I visited the church at Guca Gora, and then fighting was over in that area and the area was controlled by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you conduct an extensive investigation of religious sites on both sides while you were present as an ECMM monitor?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every time when allegations were made about damage being done to holy places like churches and mosques, we used to check that, to check those allegations, that same day or the day after. The general opinion is a lot of mosques were destroyed or damaged, and only very few cases there was damage, small damage, found on Catholic churches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you range as far down as Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because that wasn't my area of responsibility. I didn't work in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you range as far down as Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Kiseljak was the furthest south.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You can't throw any light upon conditions relating to religious sites, for example, in towns such as Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not I myself, but I'm sure other monitors can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll move on, sir. Thank you.. Now, you gave some testimony regarding what you described as HVO propaganda or misinformation, and you are of the view that the HVO supposedly used propaganda to try to incite fear in their own people, the Croats, to try to persuade them to migrate to Croat-held territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you see any radio or TV programmes yourself?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't understand them myself, so I was informed by either my interpreter or by the locals themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In other words, you relied upon your understanding of the term "propaganda", or whatever this propaganda consisted of, upon descriptions from other people?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Being my interpreter, yes. The conclusion of propaganda I drew myself. She merely told me what was said on the radio; for instance, in Grahovici, where Father Stjepan and myself and a group of representatives of the Croat community, with their own eyes, saw their own houses undamaged and, with their own eyes, saw that there was no more danger. And we organised an escort back for these people, and that same night a radio broadcast convinced a group of these people that it was unsafe to go. So I then realised that this must have been propaganda, even if I didn't hear it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was the night of April the 25th, 1993, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was late April, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right after the Miletici incident?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure when that happened, but it might be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were asked a question about this document that was marked as Z696, which has three signatures all apparently by the same person. Let me just suggest to you that the Croatian word "za" means "for" or "on behalf of".

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I already thought about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the person who signed it signed it "Za Mr. Kostroman" and also "Za Mr. Kordic." Does that lead you to conclude that the signor, the person that signed it, was Mr. Puljic, the third person?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't make anything about this small writing, so I don't know whether he was the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Puljic? Had you ever heard of him?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He's listed as the minister of defence. Do you know what he's the minister of defence of?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you just explained this morning that it was -- then he must have been the minister of defence of Herceg-Bosna, I guess, minister of defence of the HVO, Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one second, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just put a proposition to you. You can disagree with it if you wish. Mr. Puljic was actually the minister of defence for the Vitez area, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do I understand you correctly to say that in your view, with respect to the hostilities that occurred in the Kakanj area in the middle of June -- and there is not any doubt that hostilities did occur there, is there, sir?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I experienced about those hostilities on my way to Kiseljak to fly to my leave destination, so that's the only experience I have in this part of middle Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you know that there were about 15.000 Croat refugees that flooded out of the town of Kakanj in --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed about that when I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And is it your view that that was the result of propaganda or the result of being shot at?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't have any specific information about the incident in the area of Kakanj/Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In the middle of June, on June the 8th, actually, an ABiH offensive in Travnik started, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was more or less the offensive outside Travnik to secure the road from Travnik to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And four days later, there were about 11.000 refugees flooding out of Travnik, and they were Croats, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. According to my point of view, the majority of these 11.000 came from the Guca Gora area and not from Travnik itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But they were Croats nonetheless, weren't they, sir?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Are you of the view that, once again, those 11.000 refugees left their homes as a result of propaganda rather than as a result of being shot at by people that wanted to kill them?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't agree with you, because these people started moving already on the 8th of June and some groups on the 7th of June. It was already -- we had warnings by Croats and HVO that it was going to happen already on the 6th of June, so we had warnings. And there were no -- there was no evidence that these people had been shot at. There were no -- except for this one man in Guca Gora, there were no injuries or casualties, so I don't think you can state that these 11.000 people fled because others were shooting at them. They were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I thought I heard you say this morning, and maybe I was wrong, that there were, in fact, about 130 casualties that you visited at Nova Bila hospital resulting from that.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The majority of those casualties came from the front lines, being wounded soldiers. I only recall one small girl being injured. A very sad case, of course. That's the only civil casualty I recall from those 130 in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident, sir, in Vitez where eight boys and girls were blown apart by an artillery shell on June the 10th?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed of that. I didn't see it myself, but I was informed, yes. At a school yard, at a basketball field, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: By the way, that was the day before the Convoy of Joy was apprehended, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I doubt the witness can remember these precise dates.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there during the Convoy of Joy because I was on leave, so it must have been on the 11th or the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it's not really fair, after all this time, to ask him to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen the special report on Croats in Zenica that was dated April the 20th and April the 21st of 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher would show you Exhibit 25/1. D25/1, sorry.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read the contents as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that you can read this relatively quickly. I just would like to know if you were one of the ECMM monitors who actually performed the reconnaissance of these villages to evaluate the damage that had been done.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time. Later on, I visited some of these villages. But my name is not on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Have you actually had access to this document as you were performing your investigations regarding events at the villages named in here?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the document itself, but we had meetings in Zenica at the regional centre every evening where all the monitors reported their findings of that day, and I was informed by Mr. Junhov, who amongst others produced this report, about his findings in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you've got no reason to dispute the accuracy of anything that's contained in this report?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, I took Father Stjepan and some of the representatives of this community to check their own houses. Some of them were burnt but the majority were still there, and they felt it was safe to go back. So even if there was a threat on the 20th or 21st, this threat was at least less than the day I visited those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. We don't need to go into all of the details here, but there is one incident that you testified about where a crowd of civilians, I believe you said, had obstructed access to the Kruscica road, and that was caused by a lady being shot by a Muslim sniper; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she was shot in the back yard by a sniper. I guess it was a Muslim sniper, but I didn't see the incident myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've previously testified about this in the Blaskic case, and I believe what happened was that the lady was shot, her daughter tried to help her, and then the sniper shot a second time and this time killed the lady.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was a very sad case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the Kiseljak Valley fighting about which you testified, I only want to cover two issues. The first is in the village of Gomionica, when you finally obtained access to that village and the surrounding areas with your colleagues, you discovered no dead bodies of civilians, did you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually never got into Gomionica myself. I was stopped at the outskirts at one occasion by soldiers. Houses were still burning at that time, and then I didn't visit the burning houses or the burned houses myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second question I wanted to discuss with you was the village of Rotilj. I believe that you actually interviewed the commander of the HVO who had led the assault on the village. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he told me that he did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Commander Mirko Redjo; right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He told you that he had come under fire from villagers; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He explained to me what happened, and he said that one of his patrols or a group of his soldiers came under fire from one of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One of his soldiers was hit by gunfire; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: By small-arms fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the HVO then returned fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what happened after that or what he exactly told me, but the last message he gave me was that he had to burn down the seven houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you found that to be a logical reaction, did you not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, since you aren't allowed to cause more damage than needed. It's called collateral damage. And if you receive fire from small arms, then there's no necessity, in my point of view, to burn down all the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, on page 10023 of the Blaskic transcript, you were asked this question by Judge Riad: "Did he mean they were being shot at from the seven houses? Were they military zones?" Your answer was: "It could have been in a fighting zone. He came under fire, as he told us. One of his soldiers, one of his HVO soldiers, was wounded. He had to return fire, and then he said he had to burn down the houses. It was a logical reaction."

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From his point of view, but not from my point of view a logical reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you found his story, though, that he took 20 weapons from young men in that village from him, that he had launched an assault on the village and burned down seven Muslim houses, you found that story to be accurate; did you not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason to doubt it, since he was the commander on scene and he gave me this explanation himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you believed it to be true, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I visited the civilians in the village, and they didn't deny this part of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You touched briefly upon an incident on April the 19th, 1993, in which the city of Zenica was hit by artillery fire. Were you personally involved in the investigation that was performed by the ECMM into that incident?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, since I was stuck in Vitez at that moment. I couldn't leave the area of Vitez for five days, due to heavy fighting on the front lines. Fellow monitors in Zenica did the investigation. And they made a report on that. And I was informed on the results of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was that an oral report or a written report?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I was informed on that later on. I think Mr. Baggesen did the investigation, since he was an artillery officer himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Artillery officer you say?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did intel. business as well, but according to my knowledge he had an artillery background, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And would it be fair to say that you yourself did not participate in a subsequent investigation that Major Baggesen performed relating to an incident of shelling in the same city on May the 9th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't know -- I didn't do any investigations on shelling myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your view was that the HVO was generally better equipped than the ABiH, correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And yet would it be fair to say that in the summer of 1993 the HVO forces were defeated in Travnik, in Bugogno, in Fojnica, and in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell about Travnik, and they more or less handed over their positions. So I wouldn't call that a defeat. It's a decision of the forces themselves to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you follow events in the city of Vares in the early part of November of 1993, or don't you know --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall it, since I didn't make any notes on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember immediately before the Travnik offensive, the members of the Croat delegation to the joint operations command telling you that Croats generally did not feel safe in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was mentioned at the end of May and the beginning of June. And we transmitted this feeling of Croats to the commander of the army of BiH side and to Mr. Merdan. That's the reason why we organised mixed police patrols in the city of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I was a little bit unclear regarding some evidence that you gave regarding events in early June. I understand what you said about the HVO headquarters, but isn't it true that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually seized control of governmental buildings in that city in the early part of June?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's true. I think they controlled most of the buildings in the centre of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And on June the 8th, I think, that you found pretty much the command of the Travnik forces in a panic and about to leave the city, leave their headquarters behind, correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by the Travnik forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The HVO forces in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were no longer in Travnik at the 8th of June. They already left Travnik at the 4th of June. And they left the positions at the front lines in the night from 7th, 8th of June. They even burned the archives, so I wouldn't say that's a defeat. If you burn archives, you know what's going to happen. You just leave your headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's normal, though, if you are performing a hurried retreat, to burn ciphers and codes and things of that --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but then you don't take that much time to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave some testimony about operations around Zepce. Isn't it true that ABiH forces launched an offensive in Zepce around June the 30th?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never have been in Zepce myself. I was informed by BritBat. They had liaison officers there, and I was informed by other monitors. And Mr. Nakic and Mr. Merdan told me their side of the story about what happened in Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Zepce actually held out as a Croat enclave until the signature of the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to a very minor point, I guess. The village of Gacice that you gave some testimony about. It's true that Gacice operates the high ground in a valley opposite the village of Donja Veceriska, which operates the other high ground, and right between the two is the Vitezit factory. Both of these villages basically overlook the Vitezit factory?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Vitezit factory was a primary strategic -- was of primary strategic importance to the Croats, and to the ABiH actually, throughout all of the period that you were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed that it wasn't operational during that time, but it could be used to start up production again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were asked some questions in connection with an incident involving an UNHCR convoy on April the 28th, 1993. Let me just ask you these questions: You did not prepare any special report about this incident, did you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was mentioned in a daily report, and Mr. Thebault took over part of that daily report into his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you prepare a daily operational report yourself?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I have to look. If I have, then there's already a copy made of that. It was on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: 28th.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no report on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that there is nothing in your contemporaneous notes that mentions the name of Mr. Kordic on that date, April the 28th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you were physically present in Busovaca on that day? I think you've testified.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during the night, but I was physically present, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me turn to the second episode, the one that you testified about on July the 4th. My understanding is that you spoke initially to the commander of the military police in Busovaca, I think on June -- July the 2nd, actually, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Ljubesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then unable to achieve your objective with him, you went up the line, so-to-speak, and spoke to the HVO commander, Dusko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this chief of police said to me that he couldn't decide. He had to go to Mostar first. I tried to persuade my way of working to Mr. Grubesic, but he wasn't available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You ultimately did contact him, though, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the convoy was ultimately released at his order, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was done at his order, but we didn't reach our entire aim, since we didn't get the stolen properties back. And I was threatened by pointing a gun at myself, threatened by HVO soldiers, his soldiers. I wasn't particularly pleased by the behaviour of the brigade commander there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, no one would be pleased with that kind of behaviour. But wouldn't it be fair to say that the drivers who were apprehended were well treated?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The drivers were well treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And they had had some personal belongings taken from them, and those personal belongings were returned to them when they were released?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But after long negotiations. But we got them back finally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And your conclusion was that the military police had been overruled by the military commander in the theatre; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because my personal opinion was that this commander, this military police commander, only used going to Mostar as an excuse. And he didn't show up the next day. And as of that moment I only dealt with soldiers and officers of the HVO in Busovaca. And they were the ones who threatened me, and they were the ones who didn't return good. So that's my belief, that they overruled and took over the whole incident. Maybe they even started up the incident. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave some testimony to the effect that as far as you knew the events at Ahmici were never the results or never made the object of any investigation on the part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but they never reported any results of any investigation. We asked them to several times, and we didn't get any results.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, isn't it true that the HVO informed the ECMM that an investigation had in fact been started?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They spoke about that, but there were no results of that investigation, even if it had really started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you have any communications with Colonel Stewart or anyone at the British Battalion regarding a request that had been made and directed to Colonel Blaskic to set up an investigating commission, and that for any commission to have credibility in the international community's eyes, there should be a Muslim component on the commission too?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that I discussed with Colonel Stewart the whole incident of Ahmici. He was very upset. He showed that on television as well. He told me that he wouldn't let it as it was, that he would do his best to find the persons guilty for this incident. And, well, I couldn't check on the battalion commander, of course, but I reckoned that he would support investigations, if asked to. Later on the ECMM and the U.N. sent investigators of their own. And I met one of those investigators in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just turn to that subject before I get into the investigation subject in just slightly more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did the witness give any evidence about Ahmici? Mr. Nice, perhaps you can recollect. I don't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't recollect his giving any evidence about Ahmici. I might be wrong. Let's check it. Or if it was, it was tangential at the best. I think my recollection is the word "Ahmici" certainly may have fallen from his lips at some stage, but not in any detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, this is precisely the point. There are a lot of other witnesses who give evidence about Ahmici. You can call evidence about it. It's not going to assist unless there is a particular matter which this witness can deal with. If it's general cross-examination, which is a matter which we've heard often enough, it isn't going to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I heard the witness say that, as far as he was aware, no investigation into the events at Ahmici had been performed or no investigative efforts had ever been made by the HVO. But if the Trial Chamber's recollection is to the contrary, I am delighted to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You may be right, in which case the first point doesn't hold. But the second point does, that we've heard a very great deal and will be hearing much evidence about it. And you can call your evidence on the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The final topic of questions that I have for you, Colonel, I'm sure you'll be delighted to learn, concerns the -- I think one of the last pieces or subjects that you covered. You mentioned that you had seen someone wearing a uniform of the Croatian armed forces, the HV?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HV badge, yes, the chequerboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You saw a total of five people wearing such uniforms throughout your --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Different occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But you were only asked one question about it, correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I wasn't always in the opportunity to ask all those --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And his response to you was that he found that uniforms were hard to obtain, so basically soldiers were getting anything that they could lay their hands on. And the same is true of the members of the 325th Mountain Brigade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: German flags on their skirts you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, that German flag was being sported by Mr. Sifet Sivro --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what you mean. I was asked about that during the Blaskic case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I think you agreed that that didn't make him a member of the [indiscernible]?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Sifet Sivro was from the ABiH side?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I must add to that. That on the HVO side soldiers usually wore better uniforms and were better equipped than on the ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the single sighting of the mil 8, was it, or HIP helicopter --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Helicopter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- you saw. You do not know what operations that helicopter was involved in, do you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that specific day. I know about negotiations, about the evacuation of wounded, and later on these evacuations were organised with the acceptance of both sides. And at those occasions helicopters have been used legally or officially announced. And this one was not announced to either ECMM or British Battalion

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If it please the Court, I have no further questions for Colonel Morsink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Colonel Morsink. My name is Bozidar Kovacic and I am the counsel of Mario Cerkez. Me and my co-counsel, Mr. Mikulicic. And if I may, I should like to ask you some questions. We shall be using different languages, so can you please make sure to pause between question and answer so as to facilitate the interpreter's job. Now, Mr. Morsink, you answered briefly a question about your preparations to go to Bosnia as an EC monitor, but did you have any full knowledge, any knowledge about Bosnia-Herzegovina before that? Did you know anything about Bosnia-Herzegovina before that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal experience with Bosnia-Herzegovina is from a long time ago when I visited with my parents during holiday. And the rest of the information I got from newspapers and articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And at that time during that private visit and the preparations you underwent later, did you get the impression that it was an exotic environment, put it that way, quite different from western standards, from western ways of thinking, from western social concepts?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall it, it was a mixed community, with all kinds of ethnical backgrounds. But they lived in good harmony together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But in that context, during your briefings you also understood the differences in the religion and culture of individual or, rather, three peoples that existed in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was thoroughly briefed on the ethnical and religious backgrounds during my preparation, the 14 days in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't recall hearing something about your military qualifications before you came to Bosnia. Of course, I don't really want to go into that, unless absolutely necessary. But I should like to ask you, had you been trained in intelligence or reconnaissance skills?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have specific intelligence training, but as a tank platoon commander, and as a company commander, and later on as a signal officer in the battalion command level, and during my war college study in The Hague, we learned a lot about former Warsaw Pact material and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I trust you don't mean by this that the former Yugoslavia, whose successors were the armies that we're talking about, that Yugoslavia was a member of the Warsaw Pact, do you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course I don't mean that, but it's just to state that I know how to recognise military equipment. And during my training, special training, the 14 days in The Hague, we had a few lessons on how to identify material and equipment used in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During the time you received your education and training or at any time, and especially at the time when you were receiving military training, did you have some particular course in verbal communication with people? I mean how to approach and how to communicate with foreign cultures.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communication is a common training at the military academy and later on at the war college, and during the 14 days' course in The Hague, we had a special training on how to negotiate with people and how to use interpreters within these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: To conclude this part of my questions, we shall agree, I suppose, that the most important thing in negotiations is to ensure -- to see to it that the parties do understand one another, that they do get across.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. If you want to transmit a message, then you have to check whether this message is received or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Needless to say, to have to work through an interpreter, I must say, through what I heard and saw in various videotapes of those interpreters you had down there on the ground, that must have been an aggravating circumstance in mutual communication. Would that be true?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You constantly needed your full attention to be able to understand what was said and to think about the next question or the next item to discuss about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you will agree that if we were in your place, any one of us would have communicated better, if we were placed in a situation, to speak the same language as the other party?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The difference in language was a problem to work with, but we had good, skilled interpreters, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] Right. Now, let us change the subject. On the 16th, you arrived in Central Bosnia, and on the 17th, you found yourself in the middle of a storm, if I may put you that way. Now, that first day, the 17th, you already had the first meeting with Cerkez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you told us that on that first occasion, Cerkez was introduced to you as the commander of a Domobran, of a home guard brigade, and you said that that brigade's name was Stjepan Tomasevic. To try to expedite matters a little, later on in your statement, you refer to the same brigade but called it the Vitez Brigade. Now, could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that I was not aware of the fact that it was a home guard brigade. They never introduced themselves as that. This name of the brigade I got from the operational chart, I got from the intel. cell, which is being used as a source of information during this meeting here. I used the name Vitez Brigade for myself just to make a distinction between the vicinity of Vitez and Busovaca and the other cities, since nearly every municipality had their own brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, if I understand you properly, you used the word "Vitez" and this adjective to simply identify the affiliation of a brigade with a particular place, with a particular locality. Would that be correct to say?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was not the only one to use it that way; also the British officers. And amongst these others, we spoke about the Viteska or the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But at that time on the ground, I mean in Vitez, there was a unit which appeared from time to time which was called Vitezovi. You mentioned it some time towards late in your testimony; is that true?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Referring to this unit of Vitezovi, I do not mean the same unit as the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when did you learn that they were not one and the same thing?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already quite early in the conflict, I was told that the Vitezovi was a kind of special unit within the structure of the brigade or maybe within the structure of the operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the 17th, the first time you spoke to Cerkez, you didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This has also to do with the conversation which you also touched upon with Mr. Kordic's counsel, and could we again -- I should like to ask the usher to take out back again Z2535/1. That is an organogram which you had a moment ago before you, and if I am correct, you told us that you received that from your colleagues in the BritBat. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you what period of time it referred to?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is it on the chart?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, no. It is not on the chart, but did anyone tell you to which period of time it could refer?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you say the name again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, there must be some misunderstanding. My question is, and perhaps I didn't phrase it properly, but my question is whether your colleagues in the British Battalion, who gave you this chart, did they tell you to which period of time this chart -- this HVO chart applied? When did they have that kind of organisation?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I got the information from this intel. officer I think at the end of April, maybe at the beginning of May, and they didn't fill in all the names. So it was kind of a first raw sketch, and they asked us to check on those names, since we always reported in our daily reports whom we met with. And if we could come up with additional names, then they would fit them within this organogram. So it's supposed to be an actual scheme, and they didn't tell me anything about what happened before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Let us not waste too much time with it. I shall tell you what I know, and you can then agree with me or disagree with me. This chart reflects the HVO organisation sometime in late 1992, so they gave you a document which was quite outdated. Let me remind you of something, and then perhaps you will be able to help us. First, where you believed that Cerkez was the commander or, rather, a member of the command of Novi Travnik, have you ever heard that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You haven't. Secondly, this upper box to the right, "HVO Joint Commission, Travnik", it is not the commission that you spoke about. This is an attempt to set up a joint command, and you may have heard about it on the basis of the names that I mentioned here, that is, Franjo Nakic and Merdan, who were among the candidates to become commanders of it. Could that be it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain already before that the organisation in Travnik was meant to be a command and not a commission, so it's a joint command led by officers and not meant to be used as a meeting group where all kinds of requests were made. This was meant to command the troops like, for instance, the fighting at the front lines. And contrary to this, the local joint commissions were raised to solve local problems, and that was the right place to make requests. So I didn't mean to refer to the JOC as a commission. I meant to say that it should be a joint command in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you will agree with me when I say that there is no quite [indiscernible] reason to believe that this chart would also apply to April 1993, to the situation in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, I did have no reason to doubt this chart, since the British were able to work with it, and I found most of the units defined here, specified, and they were correct. And the names on the list, like Mr. Cerkez introducing himself as the brigade commander, I didn't find that untrue, so there was no reason for me to doubt this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's not the point for Cerkez. We agree for Cerkez. But he was there two or three months earlier. I'm sorry, I switched to English not purposely. [Interpretation] No, it has nothing to do with Cerkez, but Cerkez was with Stjepan Tomasevic before that in late '92 and early '93, before he became the commander of the brigade in Vitez. All I wish -- all I wish you to do is to confirm to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Looking at the organogram, unfortunately part of it is cut off at the bottom, but presumably it's saying "Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade", but the commander is described as Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was the commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No dispute about that, but not at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What dates do you say that he was the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Stjepan Tomasevic, he was commander at the end of -- the latest part of February and the beginning of March, and that is why I know that that is the wrong -- I mean the document is probably good, even if it has some errors, but it's not the April situation for HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the distinction with the Viteska Brigade? Where is that on this order?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you're saying it's something different to the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. What I'm trying to imply, Your Honours, the witness said that Cerkez was presented to him as commander of Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. He was presented as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me just see what -- the point, Mr. Kovacic, which I'm trying to work out is this: You're saying that there are two separate brigades, Stjepan Tomasevic and Viteska?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Later on. From March or towards the end of March, a new brigade was founded, and they put it in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And Stjepan Tomasevic had been in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Tomasevic remained to exist in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When do you say the new brigade was formed in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mid-March, towards the end of March. I can introduce the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And Mr. Cerkez, you say, was the commander of both?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour. Cerkez was appointed as commander of the newly-founded brigade on 24 March 1993, and that was Viteska Brigade, founded by the -- founded in Vitez, with the offices and headquarters in Vitez. What I'm trying to say, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let me get this straight. Can I say he was the commander of both? He was first commander of Stjepan Tomasevic. Then he was commander of the Viteska. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is correct, with a small difference that he was commander in Stjepan Tomasevic in Novi Travnik only about the last month of his being there. That was February. Indeed, not really -- he was factually commander, and formally, and I will introduce later, the evidence is only nominated by his commander as a representative of the commander who was transferred, so something like temporary commander. But, yes, he was in Tomasevic, he was first a member of headquarters there. Later on, practically he was commander, not formally, for about a month, and then he was transferred to Vitez. He was commander of the newly-established Viteska Brigade. If I may proceed, Your Honour, it would be easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness add anything he wants. You wanted to say something, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, we -- I mean the ECMM and, I think, also BritBat never used these additional names. We always referred to brigades with the name of the town. So that's the reason why we called it the Viteska Brigade. I was never aware of the existence of an earlier brigade in another city. For me, it was relevant that Mr. Cerkez was the brigade commander of the brigade in Vitez at that moment when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we have to check. That is a wrong statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness is giving his evidence about what he knew. Now, as far as he's concerned, it's right. Now, can we, without arguing any more about it, can we move on? You'll be able to produce some other evidence which you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I won't argue, Sir. But on this document, all the brigades are having the names and the place, and that was my point. But unfortunately, we were cut off. The only brigade which does have only the name and not the place of activity is the Stjepan Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a point you can make in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to what you said earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, we have used a lot of time to simply get to the point that this document, this chart, is outdated, that it was no longer in effect at the time we are talking about. It is, I think, linked to the period of March, I think you said, when Mr. Cerkez was a kind of provisional commander of this Tomasevic Brigade in Travnik. So tell us simply that this organogram has a certain date, but that has no importance at all because you told us that the brigades were identified by the place where they were situated. So Mr. Cerkez was the commander of the brigade in Vitez, and he was no longer, as you've just said, the commander of the brigade in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct, Your Honour, but may I continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, if I am not mistaken, you confirmed, at the beginning of your examination-in-chief, a statement contained in point 8 of the summary of the proofing material. And in answer to a question from the Prosecutor you said "Yes," but it says here that Cerkez was introduced to you as the commander of the HVO brigade in Vitez, which was called Stjepan Tomasevic, and you were in his office in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because I was under the impression that this was the name of the brigade in Vitez, based on the information on the chart. But since you explained to me that this is the name of another brigade, well, then, in fact the statement was not fully correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think we can agree now that the situation was rather confusing and difficult for those first few days on the ground for you.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't find it confusing at that moment. I found it very clear. There is one brigade in Vitez, the one I had to deal with, and the name didn't matter to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. At the time, and later on in your testimony you said, allow me to quote: "I was informed that he was the brigade commander of the Vitez Brigade." You are referring to Cerkez. And the next sentence you said: "So I drew my conclusion that he was responsible for the vicinity and town of Vitez." A couple of questions, sir: So on the basis of the fact that Cerkez was a brigade commander, you came to the conclusion that he was the person responsible for the area of Vitez, is that correct, just on the basis of that fact?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was, amongst other reasons, on the basis of these facts. The other reasons are there is a war going on, and in wartime military commanders are responsible for their area of responsibility. There are certain front lines which had been already more or less defined by the British Battalion, and the front line of this Vitez Brigade was more or less around the municipality of Vitez. That, and the fact that he was introduced as the brigade commander, gave me the opinion that he must be the one responsible for the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what was his area of responsibility? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That this was the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree -- or, rather, I as a layman, and you are a military man, do I take it correctly that a commander is responsible only for the units under his command, that is those subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As such, that is correct, yes. He is responsible for the other units, but there is a specified area in our military operations, and in this specified area, even with foreign units in that area, he is the one responsible for the area. Unless his supreme commander took over this responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And we'll come to that. But we agree that Cerkez was the commander of the brigade in Vitez called the Viteska Brigade. We have also agreed that theoretically the commander is responsible and commands only his own units under his command, and he's responsible for supervising his units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he's also responsible for what happens in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In which case, Colonel? In what cases is a higher commander responsible for everything that happens in his area of responsibility, according to theory?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is responsible for the security of his own troops and responsible for security of the inhabitants of the area, and he is responsible for his troops in the way that they have to live up to the Geneva Conventions. And if something happens like, for instance, a truck bomb or the burning down of a village within his area of responsibility, then he is the one in the first line to be responsible. He is the one to check and, if possible, he is the one to see that those things don't happen at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that the key phrase is in his area of responsibility, which means, if he's responsible for this area of responsibility, do you know that Cerkez was responsible for the whole area of Vitez municipality, and on the basis of what do you make such a statement?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my assumption that he was responsible for that area, since as of the first day I met him we started discussions about what happened in all kinds of places within the municipality and the surroundings of Vitez, and he never told me that this was out of his control; that only the people were out of his control, not the village itself. When we raised the truck bomb incident, when we raised Ahmici, he never replied that this was outside of his area of responsibility. So that gave me the impression that he was the one to speak with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Isn't it normal for a commander of his rank in that area to have information, overall information about events in that area, including about other HVO units in the area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He should have that information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Normal. That's normal. Please, is there any doubt that Cerkez's commander was Colonel Blaskic, who was commander of the operative zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no doubt in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Cerkez and Blaskic, the brigade being at a lower level, one of many, and the command of the operative zone and Blaskic at a higher level, and they had staffs and headquarters in two different buildings in Vitez itself, at a distance of some 150 metres between them. Would that be true?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, yes. I visited both headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it is correct to say that Blaskic as the commander of the operative zone was based in the hotel building, and 150 or 200 metres later we find Cerkez as commander of the Viteska Brigade with his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, and we touched upon it a moment ago, that you learnt later that in the area of Vitez there were other HVO units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Amongst others, the military police battalion and the Vitezovi units and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And those units are under the command of the operative zone, that is of Colonel Blaskic, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still not aware of that. I know that there were different units and it's normal that the operational zone has next to the brigades also battalion-size units under its command, but they were not part of this organogram. And I was not informed about the exact command lines to these battalions and other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, from a great deal of testimony we have heard that there were other units, and the ECMM and the British Battalion found it difficult sometimes to exactly establish the chain of command, but nevertheless, everything points to the fact that all units in Vitez that were physically present in Vitez were under the command of the operative zone. Would you agree with that, that this was a subject of discussion and that the overall conclusion was that they were under the command of the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the final conclusion, not that it was the subject of discussions. We tried to clear that matter, but as such it wasn't of that big importance, because Mr. Thebault and the British Battalion commander himself were dealing with the operational zone level and my team was dealing with the brigade level. So also these separate units were covered by either one of us

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I ask the Honourable Court permission to -- that certain documents already accepted in evidence should be shown to the witness, and I could tell the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you hoping to achieve now, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Those are the documents in which we can clearly see they are all issued by Blaskic in his capacity of commander of operative zone. And on all those documents, and we had many, you will remember that, exactly the units under his command on the territory of Vitez are listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you can point them out to us again in argument. The witness has given his evidence about the understanding. That's something we will have to take into account, and we'll take account of your documents too, but I don't think there is much point to be gained by further argument with the witness about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Tell us, please, Colonel, had you heard that in the territory of Vitez, during the three months that you spent there, that certain independent and special units and other brigades appeared, such as Tvrtkovci, for instance. Have you ever heard of that name?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard of that name, but I heard that so-called independent units, according to my knowledge, still under the command of Blaskic appeared in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the appearance of a brigade called Ludvig Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You have already said that you had heard of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Had you heard of a unit that called itself the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You yourself said that you had heard of the military police that was operative there?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Those units were not under the command of Mario Cerkez, were they?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that by that time. I was asked about this during the Blaskic case, and they showed me by all the orders of Mr. Blaskic in the line at the bottom that he had direct orders given to these battalions you just called. So I didn't know it at that time. I was informed about that last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You didn't know about it, and so you really came to the conclusion that Cerkez was the commander of that territory?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't mind about those units themselves. My main concern was the brigade commander being responsible for the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And, as you said, this was something that you presumed? Thank you. It was an assumption on your part?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this assumption was supported by the fact that Mr. Cerkez never objected when we asked him things about what happened in his area of responsibility. Not only the first day, the 17th, but the whole period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you said that on many occasions he did refer to extremists?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He said, "Extremists, which I cannot control." But he didn't state that they were outside his unit. He just said, "I can't control them."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mentioning that, did you ever gather from that conversation, when he used the word "extremists," did he mean units, individuals or some sort of organised or independent units? Did you ever ask him what he meant when he used the term "extremists"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We discussed a lot about that. And most of the times he referred to individual soldiers being out of control. And we used to counter that argument by, for instance, the same example as I already used, that artillery cannot be operated in a proper way by using extremists or people out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You yourself said in your testimony that you didn't know whether the artillery was under the command of the brigade or the operative zone level; is that true?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But when artillery is working in close cooperation with front-line troops, then there must be a connection between brigade and operational zone level, even if this artillery is under operational zone command. Because it is in support of troops at local sites at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you are talking about theory, a theoretical model?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't believe it was only theory in Bosnia at that time. There was heavy fighting going on, and front-line troops were supported by artillery, and sometimes artillery was used as a method to fire single shells in the middle of a city. That is not supported of front-lines troop, of course, but the rest of the fightings I experienced -- for instance, around BritBat camp, that was purely supported front-line troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, of course we agree that there was artillery and that they were active, but my question is: Do you have any facts to support your claim, and you say that there are two options as to whom the artillery belongs to, do you have any facts to offer the Court from which it can be clearly seen that the artillery was under the command of the brigade, since there is a document showing the opposite?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot define whether they were under control or command of the brigade or the operational zone or maybe both. That's also possible. They both could have their own artillery

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. May I just point out, Your Honour, since I believe that it's a very sensitive question, that we have seen on many documents introduced already, and let's not waste time with those documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kovacic, this sounds to me like argument --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just wanted to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During those first few days in Vitez, did you learn anything in detail about the structure of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't learn in detail, but I was introduced to the other subordinate commanders when they showed up in meetings, and at several occasions I met single commanders at the local sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that particular officers were introduced to you or, rather, members of the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's hard to say. I didn't meet those people in the headquarters themselves. I met them on the ground when we visited parts of -- when we visited hot spots, like, for instance, the attempt to clear the houses around the BritBat camp. Those soldiers were led by an HVO officer, which later on showed up during the first meeting of the local joint commission. So I got the opinion that this man would be a commanding officer subordinate to Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned that. But will you please answer my questions. Perhaps we'll be through more quickly. We'll come to that. Let us go back to the structure. Had you ever heard how many battalions or companies there were within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion, on the basis of any facts or information, to make any conclusions regarding the strength, the effectives (sic) of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't make any attempts myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find out what sector of responsibility was assigned to the brigade, at least during the first few days of the conflict in April?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need to, since I already explained that Mr. Cerkez answered on all our questions, and he never rejected or objected and said, "That's outside of my responsibility." So there was no need to exactly specify this area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it's now 4.15. Is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How much longer do you think you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe a couple of hours. I believe I can spend tomorrow's morning, particularly because the witness is volunteering, sir. I am asking a simple question. He is repeating the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure about that. I mean, we must get on. You've had three quarters of an hour tonight. Try and deal with it more quickly tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, I can do my best. I can promise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At least by the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt. May we possibly have the dates that the Chamber won't be able to sit in November, as soon as possible, in order to help with planning witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Tomorrow morning, please. Half past 9.00.
